tagline.text: A white hilltop monastery enshrining a relic of the True Cross

children.text: A Catholic monastery atop Mount Resurrection, about 300m above sea level at the foot of the Zambales Mountains. It houses a relic rarely found in Asia, said to be a fragment of the True Cross of Jesus, and pilgrims are welcomed by a Risen Christ statue about 9m tall and a view blending mountains and plain.

Monasterio de Tarlac is a Catholic monastery atop Mount Resurrection, in Barangay San Jose de Urquico in the west of Tarlac province, where the Zambales Mountains descend to the plain. It is run by the monastic community of the Servants of the Risen Christ, founded on
September 14, 1998
, and its present church was consecrated on
January 30, 2007
. The monastery grounds have been developed as the Mount Resurrection Eco Park, with white church buildings and statues scattered among green forest and rocks. It is
45 minutes–1 hour
by car west of the provincial capital, Tarlac City, and about
140km
from Manila, making it a good stop for a day during a Central Luzon trip.

What draws pilgrims from all over the country is the True Cross relic enshrined in a golden reliquary beneath the church altar. Said to be a fragment of the cross on which Jesus was nailed, the relic is known to have been brought from Germany and is presented as the only True Cross relic in Asia. Normally, after Mass you can place a hand on the reliquary and pray, and special veneration is held on
January 30
, which commemorates the relic's enshrinement, and on
September 14
, the Feast of the Exaltation of the Holy Cross.
In the hilltop garden stands a Risen Christ statue about
tall, arms outstretched, erected in
. At only about

above sea level, the surroundings are still wide open — on one side, the layered ridges of the Zambales Mountains, and on the other, the Tarlac plain and its rice fields spread out below. The breeze is cooler here than on the flatlands, making it a good place to linger for both prayer and a walk.
For pilgrims of faith, it's a Holy Week pilgrimage stop; for general travelers, it's a peaceful hilltop viewpoint. A visit takes about
1–2 hours
, easy to combine with Capas National Shrine or Mount Pinatubo, or to build into a pilgrimage itinerary continuing north to Manaoag Church in Pangasinan.

Pray before the relic, kept in a golden reliquary beneath the church altar. After Mass, you can watch the faithful take turns touching the reliquary and praying. Non-believers are welcome to observe quietly too.
The white Christ statue, about
tall, standing in the garden is the monastery's icon. The mountain range unfolding behind the statue's outstretched arms is the most popular photo composition here.
With its red roof and white walls, the chapel recalls a mountain monastery in Europe. The interior is simple but reverent, with green hills visible through the windows.
From the garden's edge and viewpoints, the Zambales Mountains show on one side and the endless Tarlac plain on the other. Go late in the afternoon to see the sunset spread across the plain.

Take a slow walk along the garden paths, where statues of Mary and various saints stand among the rocks and trees. Small gazebos and a bell-tower-shaped structure also make it a good place to walk and reflect.

Shaded benches and rest spots are scattered through the large garden, and many local families come to sit quietly with a packed lunch. Away from city noise, an hour or two in the mountain breeze gives you a real sense of pilgrimage-site calm.

During Holy Week, pilgrims flock in from across the country for Stations of the Cross prayers and continuous Masses. If you want to experience the faith event up close, this is the most meaningful time to go, but keep in mind it's very crowded.

In the dry season,
November–April
, clear skies give the best views of the mountains and plain.
December–February
has a cool mountain breeze morning and evening, pleasant to linger in, while
March–May
is hot on the flatlands but a bit more bearable up on the hill. In the wet season,
June–October

, clouds and fog often obscure the view, and heavy rain makes the mountain road slippery. That said, the wet season turns the mountain and garden a deeper green, and clouds curling around the hillside on an afternoon after rain has its own charm.
During Holy Week (usually
late March to April
), pilgrims arrive in huge numbers, the mountain road clogs, and parking is difficult.
January 30
and
September 14

, when special relic veneration is held, are also crowded days. For quiet prayer, a weekday morning is best, and visits may be restricted on the monastic community's rest days or event days, so check ahead.

The monastery has no lodging for general travelers, so most visitors come for the day. If staying over, use a business hotel in Tarlac City (about
per night), about
40 minutes–1 hour
away by car, or a hotel or resort in Clark/Angeles (about
), about
1 hour 30 minutes
away. Tarlac City lodging also fills up early during Holy Week.

Around the monastery there are only a few stalls selling drinks and simple snacks, so bring water and snacks. Many pilgrims quietly eat food they've brought at one side of the garden. For a proper meal, it's best to head to Tarlac City. Tarlac blends the food cultures of Pampanga, Ilocos, and Pangasinan, so you can try Kapampangan braised dishes alongside Ilocano vegetable dishes, and the town's malls and restaurant rows offer a wide range of Filipino food.

Recently a Pilgrim's Coffee café and a souvenir shop have opened on the grounds, where you can buy coffee and light snacks. However, the menu is mostly drinks and snacks, so it's safer to assume a proper meal is still something to have in Tarlac City.
The chapel is a place of prayer. Avoid sleeveless tops and short shorts, and refrain from photography and talking during Mass.
Mass and relic veneration times vary by day and season, and visits may be restricted on the community's rest days. Check the monastery's latest information before you go.
Mass is usually at
, with a
3 PM

Mass added on Sundays. Thursday is the monastic community's rest day and is known as a day without Mass, and the weekday Mass days change a little from time to time, so check the monastery's Facebook notices.
Veneration, touching the reliquary in prayer, usually happens after Mass. If you want to see the relic, time your visit to a Mass.
Tricycles going up from Rubigan are hard to catch coming back down. Agree on a round trip with waiting time with your driver.
The best light for view photos is a clear morning or late afternoon before sunset.
If visiting during Holy Week or a special veneration day, arrive early in the morning to avoid mountain-road congestion and parking trouble.
The hilltop has strong sun and some shadeless stretches. Bring a hat and sunscreen.
Combining this with Capas National Shrine and Manaoag Church makes for a full day's pilgrimage itinerary.
The mountain road up to the monastery is steep with many bends. If you're not an experienced driver, use a local tricycle or a car with a driver.
After heavy wet-season rain, the mountain road can get slippery or partly washed out. Postpone your visit if a typhoon or heavy rain is forecast.
Some rocks and viewpoint edges in the garden have no railing. Watch your footing when taking photos.
Areas where the religious community lives are off-limits. Follow the signage and respect the residents' privacy.
There are few amenities nearby. Bring water, cash, and simple snacks.
